docs.title: Bans and ops
docs.text: Ops run the bot's admin commands and every plugin. Banned people are ignored completely.

docs.title: Make someone an op
docs.text:
ops:
  - '$a:mal'

Use an account entry for ops. A nick on its own lets anyone who takes that nick act as an op. !op ana adds an op until the bot restarts, and !deop ana removes one.

docs.title: Ban someone
docs.text:
<mal> !ban troll
<gamebot> mal: banned troll (account trollacct)

!ban saves the entry hardest to dodge, the same way !allow does. It also takes an entry: !ban *!*@203.0.113.* or !ban $a:troll. Bans made with !ban are saved in ban_file.

Bans in the config stay there:

banned_users:
  - '$a:troll'
  - '*!*@203.0.113.7'

docs.title: Lift a ban
docs.text:
<mal> !unban troll

!unban with the nick they use now removes every ban that matches them, account and host bans included. A ban from the config comes back on restart until it's taken out of the config.

docs.title: Only answer logged-in people
docs.text:
require_account: true

The bot ignores anyone not logged in to a services account, which makes bans much harder to dodge. Guests can't use the bot at all. The server has to support the account-tag capability, and the bot logs an error when it doesn't.

docs.title: Built-in commands
docs.text: Every bot has these. They use the bot's cmd_prefix, ! by default, and their names are reserved: no plugin or recipe can take them.

docs.title: For everyone
docs.text:
Command What it does !help lists the commands, marking (no access) on those this person can't run, and the listeners. Ops-only commands show only to ops. On IRC it answers in a private message, packed into as few lines as fit !help <command> the command's help, its usage line and its arguments

disable_help turns the built-in !help off, and frees its name for a plugin's own !help command. The other names stay reserved.

docs.title: For ops
docs.text:
Command What it does !join #channel [key] joins a channel !quit [message] quits, after sending what's waiting !reload loads plugins and recipes again, with plugin_config and access from the config file. Class plugins & reload !enable <name> [where] turns a plugin, command or listener on: here, all, or a #channel !disable <name> [where] turns one off !op <who>, !deop <who> adds or removes an op until the bot restarts !ops lists the ops !ban <who>, !unban <who> bans someone, or lifts it !banlist lists the bans !allow <name> <who>... gives access to a restricted plugin or command. Grants & denies !deny <name> <who>... keeps someone off a plugin or command !revoke <name> <who>... takes back a grant or deny !access <name> shows who can use a plugin or command !recipe add <name> <reply> adds a one-line reply recipe !recipe del <name> removes a recipe

!enable and !disable, from a private message, apply everywhere. Both are saved, and last through restarts.

A timer runs in no channel, so only all switches it. !disable notes in a channel turns off the notes plugin's commands and handlers there and leaves its timers running; !disable notes all stops them too.

Every command that changes who can do what is logged as an audit line.

docs.title: 2.0.0rc1
docs.text: The 2.0 release candidate: a new core, with 1.x plugins still running through a compatibility layer. Install it with pip install --pre pinhook.

docs.title: Before you upgrade
docs.text:
• pinhook needs Python 3.11 or newer
  • TOML configs aren't read, and relative paths in a config start from the config file's folder
  • msg.bot has only the bot's nick and channels, bot.connection is gone, and @register and @ops are removed
  • Migrating from 1.x lists every change, and shows a plugin and a config moved to 2.0

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• Plugins get ctx: who spoke, where, how to answer, and the plugin's store and settings. Handlers are async def
  • Typed commands: arguments come from the handler's signature, bad input gets a usage line, and !help <command> shows it. aliases= gives a command other names
  • Class plugins with setup(previous) and teardown(), so state carries across !reload
  • Plugins from installed packages, named in plugins and found through the pinhook.plugins entry point
  • self.bot in a class plugin, and ctx.bot, with the prefix, the data folder, and op, entry and history checks, read only
  • set_recipes and allow in class plugins, to add recipes as a plugin's own commands and give someone access to them. A grant for the whole plugin doesn't cover those recipes
  • @on for joins, parts, kicks, nick changes, topics, invites, modes, netsplits and more, and @every for timers
  • @on('addressed') for messages that start with the bot's nick, which then go to that plugin instead of running a command
  • name= on @on and @every sets the name !enable and !disable take, and !help lists @on('message') handlers with the listeners
  • An async core with an output queue, which keeps to each network's rate limits, so a slow plugin or a long reply never freezes the bot. rate_limit changes how fast it sends
  • Access levels: open, restricted or ops-only, per plugin or command, with groups, and !allow, !deny, !revoke and !access from chat
  • Recipes: commands written as YAML, which run existing commands as the person who asked, with replies, a store, loops and conditions. Ops add one-line recipes with !recipe add
  • Recipe steps from plugins can check their fields when a recipe loads, and mark text as only to be shown, never run or stored
  • IRCv3: SCRAM-SHA-256 and EXTERNAL logins, STS, server time, message tags, threaded and private replies, typing, echo-message, labeled responses, MONITOR and case mapping
  • prefix= on ctx.reply and ctx.send starts every line, split lines included
  • realname sets the name WHOIS shows for the bot
  • Twitch from a config file with platform: twitch, badges as access groups, and user IDs as accounts
  • bot.commands() lists what someone can run, bot.run_as() runs a command as them, ctx.commands() and ctx.run() do both for the sender, and ctx.history() reads a channel's recent messages
  • The command line: pinhook new, pinhook check, pinhook run, with --reload, and pinhook connect twitch
  • Deployment: an image on ghcr.io, signed and with an SBOM, ${file:PATH} secrets, secrets.env, logs to stdout and as JSON, audit lines, a health endpoint, and compose, systemd and Kubernetes examples
  • Type hints throughout, with py.typed, so mypy checks plugins against pinhook's API

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Commands are written without their prefix, and answer to cmd_prefix or the bot's nick
  • 1.x plugins run through the compatibility layer, with deprecation warnings, each on a thread of its own, one call at a time
  • Two plugins with the same command is a load error naming both
  • pinhook config.yaml is pinhook run config.yaml. The old form still works, with a warning

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• The irc library, replaced by irctokens
  • TOML configs, @register, @ops and use_prefix_for_plugins

docs.title: Before you upgrade
docs.text:
Nothing should break. Two things you might notice:

  • Plugins that use msg.bot, @register or @ops log a deprecation warning saying what to use instead (msg.bot only once per bot). They all still work. Preparing for 2.0 has the details
  • Once a plugin uses msg.store, a data/ folder appears where the bot runs, or inside bot_dir if that's set

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• pinhook.testing: a TestBot that runs your plugins without a server, so you can test them with pytest
  • msg.reply(text) and msg.send(target, text) send straight away, so a plugin can reply more than once or to several places
  • Given just the text, msg.action(text) replies where the message came from and msg.notice(text) sends the sender a notice
  • msg.account (the sender's services account) and msg.is_private
  • bot_dir keeps everything a bot uses in one folder, with plugins/, data/ and logs/ inside it. Without it, files go where they did in 1.11
  • msg.store, a dictionary each plugin can keep data in. It lasts through !reload and restarts, and is saved to data_dir automatically
  • data_dir, where plugins keep their saved data
  • plugin_config gives each plugin its own settings, as msg.config, plus a shared section every plugin can read
  • !reload also reads plugin_config from the config file again, so settings can change without a restart
  • SASL logins with sasl_password (and sasl_account if it's not the nickname). The bot is logged in before it joins channels, and gets its own nick on networks that reserve registered nicks
  • ${NAME} in a config file is filled in from the environment, so passwords don't have to be in the file
  • Docstrings for everything plugins and bot scripts use, so editors can show help, and an API reference generated from them
  • A Preparing for 2.0 guide to getting plugins ready for 2.0

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text:
• msg.bot, which will be read only in 2.0. Use msg.reply(), msg.send() and msg.botnick instead. It still works, and logs a warning once
  • @register and @ops now raise a DeprecationWarning too, saying what to use instead. They'll be removed in 2.0

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • The example dice plugins used an invalid escape in their regex, which newer Pythons warn about

docs.title: Before you upgrade
docs.text:
• SSL now checks the server's certificate. If your bot connects to a server with a self-signed certificate, it will stop connecting until you set ssl_verify: false. The log says exactly this when it happens.
  • TwitchBot connects over SSL to irc.chat.twitch.tv on port 6697, so your oauth token isn't sent in plain text anymore.
  • Bots mark themselves as bots on servers that support it. Set bot_mode: false to turn this off.
  • !ban bans accounts and hosts, not just nicks. If the person has spoken since the bot started, !ban troll bans their account if they're logged in, or their user and host if not. Bans are now saved to <nickname>.bans.json in the bot's working directory, set ban_file: "" to keep them in memory only.
  • !banlist is ops only, since bans can now include hostmasks.
  • Log lines show which bot they came from (e.g. bot.pinbot), which adds a field to the log format. Each bot now has its own logger, log level and log file.
  • log_level: off turns logging off completely. It used to still log warnings and errors.
  • Plugins are loaded as pinhook_plugins.<filename>. This only matters if one plugin imported another by its filename.
  • If you subclass Bot: call_plugins and call_internal_commands take new arguments (botnick and op).
  • Python 3.8 or newer is required.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• ssl_verify option for servers with self-signed certificates
  • bot_mode option, sets the bot user mode the server advertises
  • ops and banned_users can use hostmasks (*!*@203.0.113.7) and services accounts ($a:troll) as well as nicks
  • ban_file option, bans made with !ban last through restarts
  • require_account option, only answers people logged in to a services account
  • msg.is_op for plugins, which understands accounts and hostmasks
  • If the bot's nick is taken when it connects, it tries nick_, nick__ and so on, instead of hanging
  • When connecting fails the log says why (bad certificate, wrong port, server name typo, connection refused) instead of retrying silently
  • Unknown options are logged with a suggestion, e.g. unknown option 'ssl_requred' ignored, did you mean 'ssl_required'?
  • TOML config files work without extra packages on Python 3.11+
  • Mistakes in a config file are listed plainly, instead of as a python traceback
  • A documentation site, at https://archangelic.github.io/pinhook/
  • Tests, and a workflow running them on Python 3.8 to 3.14 (closes #10)
  • Publishing to PyPI uses trusted publishing

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• SSL crashed on Python 3.12+
  • hide=True on commands did nothing
  • !ban didn't actually stop banned users, and bans and ops were case sensitive
  • The bot didn't ignore messages from its own nick (#75)
  • Private messages crashed the bot after its nick changed
  • A plugin returning something other than message() or action() crashed the bot
  • Newlines inside a list of output lines crashed the bot
  • A plugin named like another module (e.g. json.py) replaced that module
  • log_level crashed on capital letters or warn
  • !reload left deleted plugins behind
  • Log lines were written more than once when more than one Bot was created
  • !disable said nothing for plugins that don't exist
  • !op and !ban with no nick added an empty name
  • !quit crashed when Python's site module isn't loaded
  • The toml install hint crashed instead of showing
  • Removed the enum34 dependency, which could break Python's own enum

docs.title: Class plugins & reload
docs.text:
A plugin written as a class keeps state in its instance: a connection, a cache, a counter. Its methods are its commands and handlers.

from pinhook import Plugin, command


class Counter(Plugin):
    def setup(self, previous):
        # on !reload, previous is the plugin as it was, so the count carries over
        self.count = previous.count if previous else 0

    @command('count')
    async def count_up(self, ctx):
        self.count += 1
        await ctx.reply(f'counted {self.count} times')

The bot makes one instance of each Plugin class in a plugin file. Methods take self, then ctx, then the command's typed arguments.

docs.title: Use the bot from a plugin
docs.text:
self.config is the plugin's plugin_config section, as ctx.config is, from setup on, so a plugin can check its settings as it loads. !reload reads plugin_config again, and the new instance gets the new settings.

self.bot is the bot, from setup on, and handlers get the same as ctx.bot. It's read only:

Member What it is nick, channels the bot's nick and channels prefix the command prefix, like ! logger the bot's logger, as ctx.logger data_dir the bot's data folder, for files a plugin keeps is_op(who) True if who, a Source or a Member, is one of the bot's ops matches(entry, who) True if an entry like '$a:mal' names who, as ops and bans match keeps_history(channel) True if the history option lists the channel split(target, text, prefix) the lines text would go to target as, split to fit the network

docs.title: Add recipes and grant access from a plugin
docs.text:
A class plugin can change its own commands, and nothing else of the bot's, from setup on:

Method What it does self.set_recipes(recipes) adds recipes as commands of the plugin, in place of the ones it added before self.allow(command, who) gives who access to one of the plugin's restricted commands, as !allow does

A plugin that keeps recipes somewhere other than recipe_dir adds them in setup:

from pinhook import Plugin, recipes


class Moves(Plugin):
    def setup(self, previous):
        found = [recipes.load_recipe(path) for path in self.saved_paths()]
        self.set_recipes(found)

They load after the recipe folder's, so a name a recipe file has is left out, and set_recipes returns the problems. Setting them again replaces them at once. !disable moves turns them off with the plugin, and the plugin's level and denies cover them. A grant for the whole plugin doesn't, since what a plugin adds can change after the grant: each recipe takes its own, from allow or !allow !dance carol.

allow takes only the plugin's own commands, and refuses one that's ops only, as !allow does. It returns False when they had access already, or the command is open to everyone. Each grant is logged as an audit line.

docs.title: Make one with pinhook new
docs.text:
pinhook new plugin counter

This makes plugins/counter.py, a class plugin, and tests/test_counter.py, a passing test for it.

docs.title: Reload without restarting
docs.text:
!reload, from an op, loads every plugin and recipe again:

  1. The bot makes a new instance of each class and calls its setup(previous) with the old instance, so it copies across what it wants to keep
  2. It calls the old instance's teardown()
  3. Commands, handlers and timers switch to the new code

setup gets None as previous the first time a plugin loads. teardown also runs when a plugin is removed and when the bot quits. Take anything that has to stay open away from the old instance, so its teardown doesn't close it:

def setup(self, previous):
    if previous:
        self.conn, previous.conn = previous.conn, None
    else:
        self.conn = open_connection()

def teardown(self):
    if self.conn:
        self.conn.close()

ctx.store lives through a reload without any of this, since it's saved to disk.

docs.title: Load a plugin from a package
docs.text:
Install the package, then name its plugin in plugins:

pip install pinhook-dice

plugins:
  - dice

The name is the plugin's own: it names its store, its plugin_config section, and what !enable and !disable take. !reload makes new instances of its classes, and calls setup(previous) as it does for files. Code from an upgraded package loads when the bot restarts.

docs.title: Publish a plugin as a package
docs.text:
Point a pinhook.plugins entry point at the module holding the plugin's handlers and classes, in pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."pinhook.plugins"]
dice = "pinhook_dice.plugin"

dice is the name bots list in plugins. The module uses the 2.0 API: @command, @on, @every and Plugin classes, defined in that module.

docs.title: Reload on every save
docs.text:
pinhook run --reload config.yaml

The bot reloads whenever a plugin or recipe file is added, changed or removed, for development.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
pinhook makes bots, checks them and runs them.

Command What it does pinhook new bot NAME makes the folder NAME/: a config, an example plugin and its test, and recipes/, data/ and logs/ pinhook new plugin NAME makes plugins/NAME.py, a class plugin, and tests/test_NAME.py pinhook new recipe NAME makes recipes/NAME.yaml pinhook check [CONFIG] checks the config, plugins and recipes without connecting pinhook run [CONFIG] connects and runs the bot pinhook connect twitch [CONFIG] saves a Twitch token in secrets.env pinhook --version the installed version

CONFIG is config.yaml in the current folder unless given.

docs.title: pinhook new
docs.text:
new plugin and new recipe offer to open the new file in an editor: $VISUAL or $EDITOR, or a list of the editors on the PATH. --edit opens it without asking, and --no-edit just saves it. Outside a terminal, the file is just saved.

The templates ship inside pinhook, so what new makes matches the installed version.

docs.title: pinhook check
docs.text:
pinhook check config.yaml
pinhook check --strict config.yaml

check loads the config and its plugins and recipes the way run does, without connecting. Plugins' setup runs, then their teardown. It lists every warning and error, and fails on errors. --strict fails on warnings too, for CI.

docs.title: pinhook run
docs.text:
pinhook run config.yaml
pinhook run --reload config.yaml

run reads secrets.env beside the config, then the config, then connects. It runs until !quit or SIGTERM, which lets running commands finish and sends what's waiting before it quits. --reload reloads plugins and recipes whenever their files change, for development.

pinhook config.yaml, with no command, still runs the bot, with a warning: the shorthand will be deprecated in a future version.

docs.title: pinhook connect
docs.text:
pinhook connect twitch config.yaml

Asks for the bot account's token without showing it, saves it as TWITCH_TOKEN in secrets.env beside the config, readable only by you, and says what the config still needs. The config is config.yaml in the current folder unless given. A script pipes the token in instead: pinhook connect twitch < token.txt.

docs.title: Config formats
docs.text: The format comes from the file's extension: .yaml, .yml or .json. --format yaml or --format json sets it for another name.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: A bot's settings live in one YAML file, config.yaml. JSON works too, as config.json.

docs.title: Write the config
docs.text:
nickname: 'gamebot'
server: 'irc.libera.chat'
port: 6697
ssl_required: true
channels:
  - '#gamebot-test'
ops:
  - '$a:youraccount'
bot_dir: '.'

nickname, server and channels are required. Options lists every setting.

docs.title: Quote channel names and nicks
docs.text:
YAML reads # as the start of a comment, and reads no, off, yes and on as true and false. Quote every channel name, and any nick that's one of those words:

nickname: 'off'
channels:
  - '#games'

pinhook check catches both mistakes and says to quote the value.

docs.title: Keep the bot in one folder
docs.text:
bot_dir puts everything the bot keeps in one folder:

gamebot/                <- bot_dir
├── config.yaml
├── plugins/            <- plugin_dir
├── recipes/            <- recipe_dir
├── data/               <- data_dir: plugin stores, bans, grants, !enable and !disable
└── logs/
    └── gamebot.log     <- log_file

Relative paths in the config, bot_dir's included, start from the folder the config is in. bot_dir: '.' is that folder, so pinhook run gamebot/config.yaml works from anywhere.

docs.title: Keep secrets out of the file
docs.text:
Write ${NAME} for a value from the environment, and ${file:PATH} for a value read from a file:

sasl_password: '${SASL_PASSWORD}'
plugin_config:
  weather:
    api_key: '${file:/run/secrets/weather_key}'

Put the values in secrets.env beside the config, readable only by you:

echo 'SASL_PASSWORD=hunter2' >> secrets.env
chmod 600 secrets.env

pinhook run reads secrets.env before the config. A variable already set in the environment wins, so a service manager or container supplies its own. $${ is a literal ${.

Values from ${...} in token, sasl_password, ns_pass, server_pass and plugin_config show as *** in the log.

docs.title: Set defaults from the environment
docs.text: PINHOOK_ variables set any single-value option the config leaves out, like PINHOOK_LOG_FILE=- for log_file. The config wins. The image sets its defaults this way. Secrets can't be set like this: they come from ${...}, so they stay masked.

docs.title: Give plugins their settings
docs.text:
plugin_config has a section per plugin file, and a shared section every plugin reads:

plugin_config:
  weather:
    units: 'metric'
  shared:
    modteam: ['mal', 'ana']

A plugin reads its section as ctx.config, and the shared one as ctx.config.shared. The context covers it.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
pinhook check config.yaml

check validates the config, loads the plugins and recipes, and lists every warning and error. It fails on errors. pinhook check --strict fails on warnings too, for CI.

docs.title: Run it from Python
docs.text:
load_bot makes the bot a config describes, the same way pinhook run does, with secrets.env, ${...} and relative paths:

from pinhook.config import load_bot

bot = load_bot('gamebot/config.yaml')
bot.start()

A mistake in the config raises ConfigError, saying what's wrong.

docs.title: Pick the platform
docs.text: platform is irc unless set. A Twitch bot sets platform: twitch. Twitch covers it.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: A bot is one long-running process holding one connection. Run it as exactly one instance: a container, a systemd service, or pinhook run.

docs.title: Run one copy
docs.text: Two copies of a bot fight over its nick and answer every command twice. Every example here runs one copy, and replaces it by stopping the old one first: strategy: Recreate on Kubernetes, never a rolling update. Restarts are safe: the bot reconnects, and its state is on disk.

docs.title: Keep state on a volume
docs.text:
data_dir holds plugin stores, grants and denies, bans, !enable and !disable, and STS policies. recipes/ holds recipes added from chat. Put both on a persistent volume with one writer. A backup is a copy of the two folders.

The config is read only. Check it in CI before it's deployed:

pinhook check --strict config.yaml

docs.title: Pass secrets
docs.text:
Write ${NAME} for an environment variable and ${file:PATH} for a file, which is how Docker and Kubernetes secrets arrive:

sasl_password: '${file:/run/secrets/sasl_password}'

secrets.env beside the config is for a plain install. A variable already in the environment wins. Secrets show as *** in the log.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
log_file: '-'
log_format: json

log_file: '-' writes to stdout. log_format: json writes one JSON object per line, with time, level, bot and message, and error with the traceback:

{"time": "2026-11-02T10:15:00.123+00:00", "level": "info", "bot": "gamebot", "message": "mal (account mal) ran !ban troll: banned troll (account trollacct)", "audit": true}

Changes to who can do what are audit lines, logged with who made them and carrying "audit": true: !op, !deop, !ban, !unban, !allow, !deny, !revoke, !enable, !disable and !recipe.

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
health_port: 8080

/healthz answers 200 while the process runs. /readyz answers 200 once the bot is connected and in every channel in its config, and 503 with the reason before then, like not in #games. It listens on health_host, 127.0.0.1 by default.

docs.title: Shut down cleanly
docs.text: SIGTERM lets running commands finish and sends what's waiting, for up to 5 seconds, then quits. Give the bot longer than that to stop: the examples give it 30 seconds.

docs.title: Network
docs.text: A bot makes outbound connections only: IRC on 6697, or Twitch's chat servers. It needs no inbound ports apart from the health endpoint.

docs.title: The image
docs.text:
ghcr.io/archangelic/pinhook is pinhook on Python 3.15's slim image, for amd64 and arm64, tagged with each version and its minor and major, like 2.0.0, 2.0 and 2. It runs as user 10001, with /bot as its folder:

Path Holds /bot/config.yaml the config, mounted read only /bot/plugins plugins, mounted or built in /bot/recipes recipes, writable for !recipe add /bot/data the volume

It runs pinhook run /bot/config.yaml, logs to stdout, and serves the health endpoint on 8080. A bot with plugin dependencies builds its own image on it:

FROM ghcr.io/archangelic/pinhook:2
COPY plugins /bot/plugins
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir requests

Each image is signed with cosign. Check one:

cosign verify ghcr.io/archangelic/pinhook:2 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/archangelic/pinhook/' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
Save these beside config.yaml, plugins/ and recipes/, with the bot account's password in sasl_password.txt, then run docker compose up -d.

compose.yaml:

# One pinhook bot. Beside this file: config.yaml, plugins/, recipes/ and
# sasl_password.txt holding the bot account's password. The bot runs as uid 10001,
# so give it recipes/ for the recipes ops add from chat: sudo chown 10001 recipes
#
#   docker compose up -d
#   docker compose logs -f
services:
  bot:
    image: ghcr.io/archangelic/pinhook:2
    # one copy only, since two would fight over the nick
    restart: unless-stopped
    configs:
      - source: config
        target: /bot/config.yaml
    secrets:
      - sasl_password
    volumes:
      - ./plugins:/bot/plugins:ro
      - ./recipes:/bot/recipes
      - data:/bot/data
    # longer than the bot's shutdown_wait, so it quits cleanly
    stop_grace_period: 30s

configs:
  config:
    file: ./config.yaml

secrets:
  sasl_password:
    file: ./sasl_password.txt

volumes:
  data:

config.yaml:

nickname: 'gamebot'
server: 'irc.libera.chat'
port: 6697
ssl_required: true
channels:
  - '#gamebot-test'
ops:
  - '$a:youraccount'
# compose mounts the secret here
sasl_password: '${file:/run/secrets/sasl_password}'

docs.title: systemd
docs.text:
For a plain pip install on a server. Save this as /etc/systemd/system/pinhook.service, after the steps at its top:

# A pinhook bot from a plain pip install, as the pinhook user:
#
#   sudo useradd --system --home-dir /srv/pinhook --shell /usr/sbin/nologin pinhook
#   sudo python3 -m venv /srv/pinhook/venv
#   sudo /srv/pinhook/venv/bin/pip install pinhook
#
# Put config.yaml, plugins/ and recipes/ in /srv/pinhook, and secrets in
# /srv/pinhook/secrets.env, owned by pinhook with mode 600. Then:
#
#   sudo mkdir -p /srv/pinhook/data /srv/pinhook/recipes
#   sudo chown -R pinhook: /srv/pinhook
#   sudo cp pinhook.service /etc/systemd/system/
#   sudo systemctl enable --now pinhook
#   journalctl -u pinhook -f

[Unit]
Description=pinhook bot
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=exec
User=pinhook
WorkingDirectory=/srv/pinhook
ExecStart=/srv/pinhook/venv/bin/pinhook run /srv/pinhook/config.yaml
# logs to the journal, and the health endpoint for a monitor to check
Environment=PINHOOK_BOT_DIR=/srv/pinhook PINHOOK_LOG_FILE=- PINHOOK_HEALTH_PORT=8080
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=10
# longer than the bot's shutdown_wait, so it quits cleanly
TimeoutStopSec=30

NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
PrivateDevices=yes
ReadWritePaths=/srv/pinhook/data /srv/pinhook/recipes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

/srv/pinhook/config.yaml:

nickname: 'gamebot'
server: 'irc.libera.chat'
port: 6697
ssl_required: true
channels:
  - '#gamebot-test'
ops:
  - '$a:youraccount'
# from secrets.env beside this file: SASL_PASSWORD=...
sasl_password: '${SASL_PASSWORD}'

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
A ConfigMap for the config, a PersistentVolumeClaim for data/ and recipes/, and a Deployment with one replica, strategy: Recreate and probes on the health endpoint:

# One pinhook bot on Kubernetes: its config, its secret, a volume for data/ and
# recipes/, and the bot itself. Plugins go in an image built on pinhook's:
#
#   FROM ghcr.io/archangelic/pinhook:2
#   COPY plugins /bot/plugins
#
#   kubectl create secret generic gamebot-secrets --from-literal=sasl_password=...
#   kubectl apply -f pinhook.yaml
#   kubectl logs -f deployment/gamebot
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: gamebot-config
data:
  config.yaml: |
    nickname: 'gamebot'
    server: 'irc.libera.chat'
    port: 6697
    ssl_required: true
    channels:
      - '#gamebot-test'
    ops:
      - '$a:youraccount'
    # the Secret is mounted here
    sasl_password: '${file:/run/secrets/pinhook/sasl_password}'
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: gamebot-data
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: gamebot
  labels:
    app: gamebot
spec:
  # one copy only, since two would fight over the nick. Recreate stops the old pod
  # before starting the new one
  replicas: 1
  strategy:
    type: Recreate
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: gamebot
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: gamebot
    spec:
      # longer than the bot's shutdown_wait, so it quits cleanly
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10001
        fsGroup: 10001
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
        - name: bot
          image: ghcr.io/archangelic/pinhook:2
          ports:
            - name: health
              containerPort: 8080
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: health
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: health
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: [ALL]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /bot/config.yaml
              subPath: config.yaml
              readOnly: true
            - name: secrets
              mountPath: /run/secrets/pinhook
              readOnly: true
            - name: data
              mountPath: /bot/data
              subPath: data
            - name: data
              mountPath: /bot/recipes
              subPath: recipes
      volumes:
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: gamebot-config
        - name: secrets
          secret:
            secretName: gamebot-secrets
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: gamebot-data

Each example is started against a real IRC server in pinhook's CI, so these files work as shown.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
@on runs a handler when something happens in a channel: someone joins, a topic changes, the bot connects.

from pinhook import on


@on('join')
async def greet(ctx):
    await ctx.reply(f'welcome, {ctx.nick}')

Handlers never see the bot's own joins or messages, so the bot never welcomes itself.

docs.title: The events
docs.text:
Event When Extra on ctx message a message that isn't a command, /me actions included text, kind addressed a message that starts with the bot's nick, like gamebot: what's on tonight? text, and arg: the message after the nick notice a notice text join someone joins a channel part someone leaves text, the reason kick someone is kicked kicked, text quit someone quits the network text nick someone changes nick new_nick. nick is the old one topic a channel's topic changes text, the new topic invite the bot, or with invite-notify anyone, is invited invited mode a channel's modes change modes, like ['+o', 'mal'] netsplit servers split and people drop off together nicks, text netjoin they come back nicks, text connected the bot has connected and is about to join its channels disconnected the bot has lost the connection

ctx.channel is the channel the event happened in, and None for events that aren't in one, like nick and quit.

docs.title: Read every message
docs.text:
@on('message') sees every message that isn't a command:

from pinhook import on


@on('message')
async def thanks(ctx):
    if 'thanks gamebot' in ctx.text.lower():
        await ctx.reply('any time')

!help lists it as a listener by its function's name, thanks, and !disable thanks turns it off. Give it another name with name:

@on('message', name='thanker')

A netsplit is one event for everyone who left, not one per person, so a bot never answers a netsplit with a flood.

docs.title: Answer when spoken to
docs.text:
@on('addressed') gets the messages that start with the bot's nick, with the rest in ctx.arg:

from pinhook import on


@on('addressed')
async def chat(ctx):
    await ctx.reply(f'you said: {ctx.arg}')

While a plugin handles addressed, gamebot: roll 2 20 goes to it instead of running roll, and commands need their prefix: !roll 2 20, or gamebot: !roll 2 20. Listeners and @on('message') handlers still see the message, with ctx.addressed set. !disable chat in a channel turns commands after the nick back on there.

docs.title: Test an event
docs.text:
from pinhook.testing import TestBot


def test_greet():
    bot = TestBot(plugin_dir='plugins')
    assert [s.text for s in bot.event('join', nick='ana')] == ['welcome, ana']

TestBot covers the other events.

docs.title: Grants & denies
docs.text: Ops give and take access from chat. Grants and denies are saved in data_dir and last through restarts.

docs.title: Give someone access
docs.text:
<mal> !allow weather carol
<gamebot> mal: gave access to plugin weather to carol (account carol)

!allow takes a plugin or a command, then one or more people or groups. A command is written with or without its prefix: !allow !weather carol.

A grant for a plugin covers its commands, but not the recipes it adds with set_recipes. Give each of those its own: !allow !dance carol.

docs.title: Keep someone off
docs.text:
<mal> !deny games troll

A deny beats a grant, and works on open plugins too.

docs.title: Take it back
docs.text:
<mal> !revoke weather carol

!revoke removes grants and denies for that person, by their nick or whatever was saved for them. Grants and denies in the config stay until they're taken out of the config.

docs.title: What gets saved
docs.text:
A nick is easy to change, so !allow, !deny and !ban save the entry that's hardest to dodge:

Platform Saved IRC their account, $a:carol, when they're logged in. Otherwise their user and host, *!*carol@203.0.113.7 Twitch their user ID, $a:12345678

Someone who hasn't spoken since the bot started is saved by nick on IRC, and the reply says so. An entry or group name is saved as written: !allow weather $a:carol, !allow weather regulars.

docs.title: Who can't be given access
docs.text:
An ops level is set only in the config, so !allow and !deny refuse it. !allow refuses an open plugin, since everyone already has access.

Every !allow, !deny and !revoke is logged as an audit line.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pinhook needs Python 3.11 or newer. Install it with pip:

pip install pinhook

This installs the pinhook command and the library. pinhook's dependencies are irctokens, click, marshmallow and pyyaml, and nothing else.

docs.title: Install the release candidate
docs.text:
The 2.0 release candidate is a pre-release, which pip installs only when asked:

pip install --pre pinhook

docs.title: Check it
docs.text: pinhook --version

docs.title: Run it in a container
docs.text:
The image ghcr.io/archangelic/pinhook holds pinhook and nothing else. Deployment covers it.

Next: Your first bot.

docs.title: IRCv3 support
docs.text: pinhook asks for each IRCv3 capability the server offers, and each one has a fallback, so a bot works the same on servers without it.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text: Capability What the bot gets Without it sasl logs in while it connects, before joining channels ns_pass to NickServ after connecting account-tag, account-notify, extended-join ctx.account on every message, and account entries for ops, bans and access accounts from WHO replies when it joins server-time ctx.time is when the server got the message the time the bot read it message-tags ctx.tags, ctx.msgid, and the client tags below no tags echo-message the bot's own lines in ctx.history(), as the server saw them its own lines as it sent them batch, labeled-response await ctx.whois(nick) matches answers to questions, and netsplits are one event WHOIS answers matched by nick multi-prefix, userhost-in-names every mode and the full hostmask of each member the highest mode, and hostmasks from WHO away-notify, chghost, setname members' away state, host and real name kept current what WHO said when the bot joined invite-notify invite events for anyone invited to the bot's channels. Some servers, like Ergo, tell only channel operators only invites of the bot cap-notify capabilities the server adds or removes while connected the list from connecting

docs.title: Client tags
docs.text:
With message-tags, three client tags work where the server allows them. ctx.supports() says which:

Feature Used by typing async with ctx.typing(): reply ctx.reply(text, thread=True) channel-context ctx.reply(text, private=True), so the client shows the private message with the channel

docs.title: Log in with SASL
docs.text:
sasl_password: '${SASL_PASSWORD}'

The bot picks the strongest mechanism the server offers: EXTERNAL with a client certificate, then SCRAM-SHA-256, which never sends the password, then PLAIN. sasl_mechanism sets one. sasl_account is the account, the nickname by default.

docs.title: Log in with a certificate
docs.text:
SASL EXTERNAL logs in with a TLS client certificate, with no password in the config:

ssl_required: true
port: 6697
ssl_certfile: 'gamebot.pem'
ssl_keyfile: 'gamebot.key'

Add the certificate's fingerprint to the bot's account first, on most networks with /msg NickServ CERT ADD.

docs.title: Strict transport security
docs.text: A server that advertises an STS policy gets a TLS connection from then on. The bot reconnects with TLS straight away, and saves the policy in data_dir/sts.json, so a restart doesn't go back to plain text.

docs.title: Other features
docs.text:
• Bot mode: with bot_mode on, the bot sets the mode the server lists for bots, so WHOIS shows it as one
  • Case mapping: nicks and channels are compared the way the server's CASEMAPPING says
  • MONITOR: when the bot's nick is taken, it watches for the nick to free up and takes it back
  • WHOX: the bot learns members' accounts when it joins, on servers without extended-join

docs.title: Migrating from 1.x
docs.text: 1.x plugins run on 2.0 through a compatibility layer, and log a deprecation warning saying what to use instead. This page lists what changed, then shows a plugin and a config moved to 2.0.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
pip install --upgrade pinhook
pinhook check config.yaml

check loads the config and every plugin without connecting, and lists what needs changing.

docs.title: What breaks
docs.text:
Change What to do Python 3.11 or newer upgrade Python TOML configs aren't read move the settings to YAML, below pinhook config.yaml is now pinhook run config.yaml the old form still works, with a warning relative paths start from the config file's folder a bot run from a different folder than its config moves its paths, or uses absolute ones msg.bot has only the bot's nick and channels, read only use msg.reply(), msg.send() and msg.botnick, and plugin_config for settings bot.connection and bot.channels are gone, and Bot no longer subclasses the irc library's bot send through plugins. A Bot subclass's on_join and other irc library events don't run @register and @ops are removed @command('!x'), and @command('!x', ops=True) use_prefix_for_plugins is retired commands answer to cmd_prefix. A 1.x command written without a prefix, like @command('roll'), needs it now: !roll two plugins with the same command is a load error naming both rename one built-in command names are reserved a plugin command called ban or another built-in's name doesn't load. help is free once disable_help is on plugins import as pinhook_plugins.<bot>.<name> a plugin that imports another by pinhook_plugins.<name> uses the new name hide=True hides a command from ops too take hide=True off commands ops look for in !help each 1.x plugin runs on a thread of its own, one call at a time a plugin that blocks holds up only its own calls, not the bot. State shared between plugins needs a lock

pytest -W error::DeprecationWarning turns each warning into a failing test that points at the line to change.

docs.title: Move a plugin to 2.0
docs.text:
A 1.x plugin:

import random

import pinhook.plugin


@pinhook.plugin.command('!roll', help_text='roll a die')
def roll(msg):
    sides = int(msg.arg or 6)
    return pinhook.plugin.message('{} rolled {}'.format(msg.nick, random.randint(1, sides)))

The same plugin on 2.0:

import random

from pinhook import command


@command('roll', help='roll a die')
async def roll(ctx, sides: int = 6):
    await ctx.reply(f'{ctx.nick} rolled {random.randint(1, sides)}')
1.x 2.0 @pinhook.plugin.command('!roll') @command('roll'), without the prefix def roll(msg) async def roll(ctx, ...), with typed arguments msg.arg, parsed by hand arguments in the signature return message(text) await ctx.reply(text) return action(text) await ctx.action(text) @listener('name') @on('message', name='name'), so !enable and !disable still know it by its name msg.store, msg.config ctx.store, ctx.config msg.is_op ctx.is_op, or ops=True on the command ops_msg='...' denied_msg='...'

The context lists everything ctx has.

docs.title: Move a Bot subclass
docs.text:
A 1.x bot that subclasses Bot reaches into the irc library, which 2.0 doesn't use. Each of those has a 2.0 replacement:

1.x 2.0 def on_join(self, c, e): and the other on_* methods a plugin with @on('join'), and the other events overriding call_help to answer !help yourself disable_help: true, then a plugin's own !help command, or a listener, answers it bot.connection.privmsg(target, text) from another thread, like a web hook bot.send_message('privmsg', target, text), which is safe from any thread settings kept on the subclass, like self.modteam, read as msg.bot.modteam a plugin_config shared section, read as msg.config.shared['modteam']

For example, a welcome on join:

from pinhook import on


@on('join')
async def welcome(ctx):
    if ctx.channel == '#tildetown':
        await ctx.send(ctx.nick, f'Welcome, {ctx.nick}!')

docs.title: Move a TOML config to YAML
docs.text:
config.toml:

nickname = "gamebot"
server = "irc.libera.chat"
port = 6697
ssl_required = true
channels = ["#games"]
ops = ["$a:mal"]

The same settings as config.yaml, with every channel name quoted:

nickname: 'gamebot'
server: 'irc.libera.chat'
port: 6697
ssl_required: true
channels:
  - '#games'
ops:
  - '$a:mal'

docs.title: Keep running 1.x
docs.text: 1.x gets security fixes as 1.12.x releases, from the 1.x branch. Pin it with pip install 'pinhook<2'.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
These work the same in a config file or as keyword arguments to Bot. nickname, server and channels are required, and everything else has a default. An option pinhook doesn't know is logged as a warning, with the closest match:

unknown option 'ssl_requred' ignored, did you mean 'ssl_required'?

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text: Option Default What it does platform irc irc, or twitch for a Twitch bot nickname required the bot's nick realname the nickname the name WHOIS shows for the bot, like 'gamebot, a bot run by mal' server required on IRC the server's name channels required the channels to join, quoted: ['#games'] port 6667, Twitch 6697 the server's port. TLS is usually 6697 ssl_required false connect over TLS ssl_verify true check the server's certificate ssl_certfile, ssl_keyfile none a client certificate, for SASL EXTERNAL server_pass none the server's password, not the bot's account password token none a Twitch bot's OAuth token rate_limit {burst: 4, interval: 2}, Twitch {burst: 20, interval: 1.5} how fast the bot sends: burst lines at once, then one every interval seconds

docs.title: ssl_verify
docs.text: Leave it on. Turn it off only for a server with a self-signed certificate. Pointing the SSL_CERT_FILE environment variable at the server's certificate keeps the check on.

docs.title: Logging in
docs.text:
Option Default What it does sasl_password none log in with SASL while connecting sasl_account the nickname the account to log in to sasl_mechanism auto PLAIN, SCRAM-SHA-256 or EXTERNAL, or the strongest the server offers ns_pass none identify to NickServ after connecting, where SASL isn't offered or fails nickserv NickServ NickServ's nick on this network

A nick that's taken gets _ added, and the bot takes its own nick back when it frees up.

docs.title: People
docs.text: Option Default What it does ops [] the bot's ops, as entries like '$a:mal' banned_users [] people the bot ignores ban_file data/<nickname>.bans.json with bot_dir, <nickname>.bans.json without where !ban saves bans. '' keeps them in memory require_account false ignore anyone not logged in to a services account access open access levels, groups, grants and denies

docs.title: Commands and plugins
docs.text:
Option Default What it does cmd_prefix ! the prefix for every command, or a list of them: ['!', '.'] address_by_nick true commands also work after the bot's nick: gamebot: roll, gamebot, roll or @gamebot roll, unless a plugin handles addressed disable_help false turn off the built-in !help, so a plugin's own !help command answers instead plugins none installed plugins to load, by name: ['dice'] plugin_config none settings for plugins: a section per plugin, and shared plugin_channels none keep a plugin, command or listener to some channels: {weather: ['#outside']} history off keep recent messages for ctx.history(): {channels: ['#games'], size: 20, minutes: 10} bot_mode true mark the bot as a bot, where the server supports it

!enable and !disable override plugin_channels per channel, and are saved.

docs.title: history
docs.text: channels lists the channels to record. size is how many messages are kept per channel, and minutes how long. History is kept in memory only, and includes the bot's own lines.

docs.title: Files and folders
docs.text:
Option Default What it does bot_dir none one folder for plugins, recipes, data and logs plugin_dir plugins where plugins are loaded from recipe_dir recipes where recipes are loaded from data_dir data plugin stores, grants and denies, !enable and !disable, STS policies

Relative paths start from bot_dir when it's set, and bot_dir itself, like every relative path, starts from the config file's folder. ~ is the home folder.

docs.title: Logs and health
docs.text: Option Default What it does log_level info debug, info, warning, error, critical or off log_file logs/<nickname>.log with bot_dir, <nickname>.log without where to log. '-' is stdout log_format text text, or json for one JSON object per line health_port off serve /healthz and /readyz on this port health_host 127.0.0.1 the address the health endpoint listens on

docs.title: From the environment
docs.text: ${NAME} in any value reads an environment variable, and ${file:PATH} reads a file. PINHOOK_<OPTION> sets a single-value option the config leaves out, like PINHOOK_HEALTH_PORT=8080. Configuration covers both.

docs.title: Retired
docs.text: use_prefix_for_plugins does nothing in 2.0, and logs a warning: plugin commands always use cmd_prefix.

docs.title: Templates & filters
docs.text:
A recipe's text is a template: {name} is a variable, and | passes it through a filter.

- reply: '{nick} hugs {arg|default:everyone}'
- reply: 'games: {store.games|sorted|join:, }'

{{ and }} are a literal brace.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
Filter Gives Example join a list's items, joined with ,, or the text after : {members|join: and } sorted a list, sorted without regard to case {store.games|sorted} count how many items {members|count} here first, last the first or last item {rolled|first} random one item at random {members|random} upper, lower the text in upper or lower case {nick|upper} default the text after : when the value is empty {arg|default:everyone}

Filters run left to right: {store.games|sorted|first} is the first game alphabetically.

docs.title: Read saved values
docs.text: {store.games} reads the key games from the recipes' store. {saved.key} reads a key from a dict a step saved. A missing key is empty.

docs.title: Add a filter from a plugin
docs.text:
A plugin adds filters for every recipe to use:

from pinhook import recipes


@recipes.template_filter('shout')
def shout(value, arg):
    return str(value).upper() + '!'

value is the variable, and arg is the text after :, or None.

docs.title: Add a step from a plugin
docs.text:
A plugin adds step types the same way. Each declares its fields, so recipe files using it are checked when they load:

from pinhook import recipes


@recipes.step('weather', {'weather': 'template', 'save': 'name'}, saves='save')
async def weather(run, fields):
    forecast = await fetch_forecast(run.render(fields['weather']))
    run.save(fields.get('save'), forecast)

A field's kind is one of template, text, name, path, steps, flag or any. check looks a step's fields over when its recipe loads, and returns what's wrong, or None, so a mistake in a field of kind any is caught before the recipe ever runs:

def known_units(fields):
    if fields.get('units') not in (None, 'metric', 'imperial'):
        return 'units should be metric or imperial'
    return None


@recipes.step('weather', {'weather': 'template', 'units': 'text'}, check=known_units)

docs.title: Mark text to show only
docs.text:
A step that saves text people should see but nothing should act on, like text a model wrote, marks it:

@recipes.step('guess', {'guess': 'template', 'save': 'name'}, saves='save')
async def guess(run, fields):
    run.save(fields['save'], {'kind': 'bug', 'summary': await summarise(run)})
    run.mark(fields['save'] + '.summary', '[guess] ')

A reply that uses {g.summary} starts every line with [guess]. A command, store or when that uses it stops the recipe, and a for_each over a marked list marks each {item}. Saving over a variable clears its marks. run.marked(template.paths) tells a step of its own whether a template uses marked text.

docs.title: TestBot
docs.text:
TestBot runs the real bot on a fake network: plugins, recipes, access and the built-in commands all work, with no server and no waiting on rate limits. Stores live in memory, data_dir is a new folder removed with the bot, and a plugin that raises fails the test.

from pinhook.testing import TestBot


def test_roll():
    bot = TestBot(plugin_dir='plugins')
    assert bot.say('!roll 3 1', nick='ana') == ['ana rolled 3 [1, 1, 1]']

docs.title: Say something
docs.text:
Call Sends Returns bot.say(text, nick='ana') a channel message the bot's replies in that channel bot.action(text, nick='ana') a /me the bot's replies in that channel bot.private(text, nick='ana') a private message the bot's replies to them

channel= picks the channel, the first of channels by default. account=, user= and host= say who's speaking, for ops, bans and access:

bot = TestBot(plugin_dir='plugins', ops=['$a:mal'])
assert bot.say('!reload', nick='mal', account='mal') == ['Plugins reloaded']

docs.title: Check what else it sent
docs.text: bot.sent_to('ana') is everything the bot sent to ana, like !help's private reply. bot.sent is everything it sent, as Sent records with kind, target and text.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
bot.event('join', nick='ana')
bot.event('kick', nick='mal', kicked='troll', text='bye')
bot.event('nick', nick='ana', new_nick='ana_')
bot.event('mode', nick='mal', modes=['+o', 'ana'])

Each returns what the bot sent, as Sent records. A mode change gives the member that mode, the way a real one would.

docs.title: Timers
docs.text: Time stands still until the test moves it. bot.tick(1800) lets 30 minutes pass, runs the @every timers that come due, and returns what they sent.

docs.title: Stores and settings
docs.text:
bot.store('dice') is the dice plugin's store. TestBot takes the bot's options, like plugin_config, access and recipe_dir:

bot = TestBot(plugin_dir='plugins', recipe_dir='recipes',
              plugin_config={'weather': {'units': 'metric'}})

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A plugin that raises, or one that can't load, fails the test with a PluginError and the plugin's traceback.

docs.title: Type-check plugins
docs.text:
pinhook ships its type hints. Run mypy on your plugins to catch mistakes like ctx.reply(42) or ctx.acount before the bot runs:

mypy plugins

docs.title: The context
docs.text:
Every handler gets ctx: who spoke, where, how to answer, and the plugin's own data and settings. It's the only thing a handler needs from the bot.

from pinhook import command


@command('whoami')
async def whoami(ctx):
    who = ctx.account or 'not logged in'
    await ctx.reply(f'{ctx.nick} in {ctx.channel}, account: {who}')

docs.title: Who and where
docs.text: Attribute What it holds ctx.nick, ctx.user, ctx.host who sent it ctx.account their services account, or None. On Twitch, their numeric user ID ctx.source the same, as one Source, for bot.run_as ctx.channel where to answer: the channel, or the sender for a private message ctx.is_private True for a private message to the bot ctx.is_op True for one of the bot's ops ctx.is_chanop True for a channel operator (+o or above) in this channel ctx.is_bot True when the server marks the sender as a bot ctx.addressed True when the message started with the bot's nick, like gamebot: roll ctx.text the whole message ctx.command, ctx.arg the command's name, and everything after it. For @on('addressed'), the message after the bot's nick ctx.time when it was sent, the server's time when it says ctx.tags, ctx.msgid the message's IRCv3 tags and ID ctx.bot the bot's nick, channels, prefix and more, read only ctx.logger the bot's logger

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
await ctx.reply('done')                      # where the message came from
await ctx.reply('done', thread=True)         # as a reply to this message
await ctx.reply('just you', private=True)    # a private message to the sender
await ctx.action('waves')                    # a /me
await ctx.notice('a notice to the sender')
await ctx.send('#announcements', 'liftoff')  # anywhere else
await ctx.reply(forecast, prefix='[wx] ')     # every line starts with [wx]

A string with line breaks, or a list, is sent a line at a time. Every line goes through the output queue, which keeps to the network's rate limits, so a long answer never floods the bot off the server.

thread=True uses the IRCv3 reply tag where the server supports it, and starts the line with the sender's nick elsewhere. prefix starts every line, including each part of a line split to fit the network.

docs.title: Show it's working
docs.text:
async with ctx.typing():
    forecast = await fetch_forecast(city)
await ctx.reply(forecast)

Clients that show typing notifications show the bot typing until the block ends.

docs.title: Save data
docs.text:
ctx.store is a dict saved as JSON in data_dir after each run of the handler, and kept between reloads and restarts. Each plugin file has its own:

@command('count')
async def count(ctx):
    ctx.store['count'] = ctx.store.get('count', 0) + 1
    await ctx.reply(f"counted {ctx.store['count']} times")

Values are what JSON holds: strings, numbers, lists, dicts, True, False and None.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
ctx.config is the plugin's section of plugin_config, read only. ctx.config.shared is the section every plugin reads.

@command('weather')
async def weather(ctx, city: str):
    units = ctx.config.get('units', 'metric')
    ...

ctx.config['api_key'] for a setting that isn't there raises an error naming the setting and the plugin.

docs.title: The channel's people
docs.text:
ctx.members()            # everyone in this channel, as Members
ctx.member('ana')        # one Member, or None
await ctx.whois('ana')   # asks the server, and waits for the answer

A Member has nick, account, modes, is_chanop, is_voiced, away and is_bot. members() comes from what the bot already knows, so it never waits.

docs.title: Recent messages
docs.text:
ctx.history() is this channel's recent messages, oldest first, for channels the history option lists:

for entry in ctx.history(limit=5):
    ctx.logger.info(f'{entry.nick}: {entry.text}')

docs.title: Run commands as the sender
docs.text:
ctx.commands() lists the commands the sender can trigger here, as the command listing gives them: name, help, typed arguments and access level. await ctx.run('roll', '2 20') runs one as the sender, with their access, and returns a RunResult holding what it said, instead of saying it:

@command('quietly')
async def quietly(ctx, name: str, arg: str = ''):
    result = await ctx.run(name, arg)
    await ctx.reply(f'{name} {result.status}: {len(result.lines)} lines', private=True)

A command the sender couldn't run themselves comes back refused.

docs.title: What the network supports
docs.text: ctx.supports('typing'), ctx.supports('reply'), ctx.supports('notice') and ctx.supports('private') say what this network does. On Twitch, notices to people and private messages aren't sent, so ctx.reply(private=True) answers in the channel.

docs.title: Timers
docs.text:
@every runs a handler on a timer, while the bot is connected.

from pinhook import every


@every(minutes=30)
async def reminder(ctx):
    await ctx.send('#games', 'game night is friday at 8')

A timer has no channel or sender, so it answers with ctx.send(target, text).

docs.title: Set the interval
docs.text:
@every(seconds=..., minutes=..., hours=...) adds them together. The first run is one interval after the plugin loads, and !reload starts the count again.

A run still going when the next one is due is left to finish, and the next run waits for the one after.

docs.title: Turn a timer off
docs.text:
!disable reminder stops it everywhere, since a timer runs in no channel, and !enable reminder starts it again. Disabling its whole plugin in a channel leaves it running; !disable <plugin> all stops it. The name is the function's. Give it another with name:

@every(minutes=30, name='friday')

docs.title: Test a timer
docs.text:
Time stands still in TestBot until the test moves it:

from pinhook.testing import TestBot


def test_reminder():
    bot = TestBot(plugin_dir='plugins', channels=('#games',))
    assert bot.tick(1799) == []
    assert [s.text for s in bot.tick(1)] == ['game night is friday at 8']

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Most problems show up in the bot's log. pinhook check config.yaml finds config, plugin and recipe problems without connecting, and log_level: debug logs every line the bot sends and receives.

docs.title: Starting up
docs.text: Message What to do config.yaml has problems: and a list fix each setting it names a channel name isn't quoted, so YAML read it as a comment quote channel names: channels: ['#games'] YAML read off as false, not a name quote the nick: nickname: 'off' config.yaml uses ${NAME}, but that environment variable isn't set set it, or add it to secrets.env beside the config other users can read secrets.env chmod 600 secrets.env unknown option 'x' ignored, did you mean 'y'? a typo. The bot starts without the option ops: *!*@host is a hostmask, which twitch doesn't use use nicks or $a: user IDs on Twitch could not load plugin x the traceback under it shows the error. The other plugins still load couldn't load a recipe: ... the message names the file, the step and the mistake. The other recipes still load !x is already a command of plugin y two plugins, or a plugin and a recipe, have the same command. Rename one

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
The bot retries a failed connection, waiting 10 seconds at first and up to 5 minutes between tries. Each failure is logged with its reason:

Message says What to do the server's ssl certificate failed verification (...). If this server uses a self-signed certificate, set ssl_verify to false the certificate isn't signed by anyone the system trusts. Point SSL_CERT_FILE at it, or set ssl_verify: false Set server to the name the certificate was issued for use the server's real name in server, not an IP address or alias This needs fixing on the server the server's certificate has expired. Tell its admins ssl handshake failed (...). Check 6667 is the server's ssl port ssl_required is on, but port is the plain-text port. Use 6697 server name not found a typo in server, or no network connection refused nothing is listening on that port the server took too long to answer the server is down, or a firewall drops the connection

docs.title: Logging in
docs.text: Message What it means logged in as x with SASL ... the bot is logged in to its account SASL login as x failed (...), check sasl_account and sasl_password the server turned the login down, and says why in brackets. The bot connects without its account ... check the client certificate is added to the account SASL EXTERNAL failed: add the certificate's fingerprint to the account the bot can't log in with SASL here the server offers no mechanism the bot has details for. Use ns_pass on this server sasl_password will be sent without ssl turn on ssl_required, and set port to the TLS port nickname x in use, trying x_ someone has the nick. Log in with SASL, so a network that keeps registered nicks for their account gives it to the bot require_account is on but this server doesn't tell the bot who is logged in turn off require_account on this server

docs.title: The bot doesn't answer
docs.text:
1. Is it a command? A command starts with the prefix, or the bot's nick: !roll or gamebot: roll. Check !help
  2. Can they run it? !access <command> shows its level and who's allowed
  3. Is it turned off here? An op turns it back on with !enable <name>
  4. Are they banned? !banlist lists bans, which match accounts and hostmasks, not just nicks
  5. Did it fail? Look for issue with command !x in the log, with a traceback under it

docs.title: While it runs
docs.text: Message What it means issue with command !x the command raised. The traceback shows where. error_msg= on the command says something in chat too !x took longer than 30 seconds, giving up waiting for it the command didn't finish in time. timeout= on the command gives it longer x returned something, 2.0 handlers answer with ctx.reply() a 2.0 handler returned a value instead of calling ctx.reply() N lines are already waiting to go to x, dropping new ones a plugin sent faster than the rate limit allows for too long. Send less, or send it in fewer lines plugin x sent a notice to y, but this network has no notices from bots on Twitch: check ctx.supports('notice') first x reads store.y, which no recipe sets a recipe reads a store key nothing writes, most often a typo

docs.title: Twitch
docs.text: pinhook runs Twitch bots over Twitch's chat servers, with the same plugins, recipes and access rules as on IRC.

docs.title: Connect the bot account
docs.text:
Make an OAuth token for the bot's Twitch account, with the chat:read and chat:edit scopes. Then, beside the config:

pinhook connect twitch twitch.yaml

It asks for the token without showing it, saves it as TWITCH_TOKEN in secrets.env, readable only by you, and says what the config still needs.

docs.title: Configure it
docs.text:
Save this as twitch.yaml:

platform: twitch
nickname: 'gamebot'
channels:
  - '#yourchannel'
token: '${TWITCH_TOKEN}'
bot_dir: '.'

A Twitch bot joins one channel, and needs no server. A token pasted with oauth: in front works too.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
pinhook check twitch.yaml
pinhook run twitch.yaml

docs.title: How Twitch differs
docs.text:
On Twitch Rate limits 20 lines in any 30 seconds, and one a second in channels where the bot isn't a moderator, VIP or the broadcaster Message length 500 characters. Longer replies are split Repeats Twitch drops a line identical to the last one, so the bot adds an invisible character to every other repeat ctx.account the sender's numeric user ID, which stays the same when they rename ctx.is_chanop True for the broadcaster and moderators ctx.action sent as /me ctx.notice a notice to the channel is sent as a message. One to a person isn't sent, and the bot logs a warning once per plugin Private replies and !help answered in the channel, addressed to the person Join and part events late, and not for everyone in a big channel

ctx.supports('notice') and ctx.supports('private') are False on Twitch, so a plugin picks its own fallback.

docs.title: Use badges for access
docs.text:
Badges are access groups: broadcaster, moderator, vip and subscriber, from each person's latest message. chanops is the broadcaster and moderators, and voiced adds VIPs.

access:
  plugins:
    clips:
      allow: [subscriber, vip]

Entries on Twitch are nicks and $a: user IDs. Hostmasks stop the bot with an error.

docs.title: Typed commands
docs.text:
A command's arguments come from its handler's signature. pinhook splits the message, converts each word to the annotated type, and answers bad input with a usage line built from the same signature.

from pinhook import command


@command('roll', help='roll dice, like roll 2 20')
async def roll(ctx, count: int = 1, sides: int = 6):
    ...
Message Runs !roll roll(ctx), so count=1, sides=6 !roll 2 20 roll(ctx, count=2, sides=20) !roll two nothing. The bot answers usage: roll [count=1] [sides=6] (count must be a whole number)

docs.title: Name the command
docs.text: @command('roll') answers to !roll. Names are letters, digits, - and _, written without a prefix. The bot's cmd_prefix is the prefix, ! by default. A message that starts with the bot's nick works too: gamebot: roll 2 20, unless a plugin handles addressed.

docs.title: Give it other names
docs.text:
@command('roll', aliases=['r', 'dice'])

!r and !dice run roll. !help lists it once, as !roll, and !help r shows its other names. Access, !enable and !disable go by the command, whichever name is used. An alias another command already has stops the plugin loading, the same as a name.

docs.title: Use the types
docs.text:
Annotation Takes str a word. The last str argument takes the rest of the line as written int, float a number bool true, yes, on or 1, and false, no, off or 0 Literal['add', 'list'] one of the listed values Optional[int], int \| None the type, or None when it's left out

An argument with no annotation is a str. Quotes group words, so with remind(ctx, when: str, what: str), !remind "next friday" play games gives when='next friday' and what='play games'.

docs.title: Describe the arguments
docs.text:
Annotated adds a description, which !help shows:

from typing import Annotated, Literal

from pinhook import command


@command('games', help='keep a list of games')
async def games(ctx, action: Literal['add', 'list'] = 'list',
                name: Annotated[str, 'the game, like azul'] = ''):
    ...

!help games answers in a private message:

<ana> !help games
<gamebot> !games -- keep a list of games
<gamebot> usage: games [action=list] [name=]
<gamebot> action: one of add, list | name: the game, like azul

A wrong choice gets the usage line and what's allowed: usage: games [action=list] [name=] (action must be one of add, list).

docs.title: Give it help
docs.text: help='...' is the line !help roll shows. Without it, the first line of the docstring is used.

docs.title: Set who runs it
docs.text:
@command('shutdown', ops=True)          # the bot's ops only
@command('weather', restricted=True)    # ops, and people given access

denied_msg='...' is what the bot says to someone who can't run it. Access levels covers the rest.

docs.title: Handle failures
docs.text:
A command that raises is logged with its traceback, and says nothing in chat. error_msg='...' says something instead. A command that runs longer than 30 seconds is given up on and logged. timeout= changes that for one command.

Each person runs one copy of a command at a time. A second !roll from them while the first is still running is ignored.

docs.title: Hide it
docs.text: hide=True leaves the command out of !help and the command listing.

docs.title: Writing recipes
docs.text: A recipe is a command written as YAML, not Python. It runs existing commands, replies, saves data, loops and checks conditions, so a bot owner who doesn't program can make their own commands.

docs.title: Write one
docs.text:
Save this as recipes/gamenight.yaml:

version: 1
name: gamenight
help: pick tonight's game and who goes first
steps:
  - command: 'quote random games'
    save: game
  - reply: 'Tonight: {game}. {members|random} goes first'

!gamenight runs the steps in order. The bot loads every .yaml file in recipes/ when it starts and on !reload. pinhook new recipe gamenight makes a starter file.

docs.title: Run commands as the person who asked
docs.text:
A command step runs a command, written without its prefix, as the person who started the recipe, with their access. A recipe can never do more than its user could. With save: name, what the command said goes in that variable, as a list of lines. Without it, it's said in the channel.

A step that can't run stops the recipe, and it says why:

<ana> !gamenight
<gamebot> gamenight stopped: ana doesn't have access to !quote

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
Step What it does command: 'roll 2 20' runs a command, and save: name keeps what it said reply: 'text' says a template store: games with set:, add:, remove: or clear: true changes the recipes' store, kept between restarts for_each: members with steps: runs its steps once per item, as {item}

Every step can carry when, which skips it unless the condition holds:

version: 1
name: addgame
help: add a game to the list, like addgame azul
steps:
  - store: games
    add: '{arg}'
    when: arg is not ''
  - reply: 'games: {store.games|sorted|join}'

when compares a variable with a value: x is y or x is not y.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Variable Holds {nick} who started the recipe {channel} where {arg} everything after the recipe's name {members} the nicks in the channel {store.key} a key in the recipes' store {item} the current item, inside for_each anything a step saved like {game} above

Every recipe shares one store, so !addgame adds what !games lists. A recipe that reads a store key no recipe sets gets a warning when it loads, naming the closest key that is set.

docs.title: Check recipes
docs.text: The bot checks every recipe when it loads: the version, each step's fields, every variable and filter. A recipe with a mistake is left out and logged, and the rest still load. pinhook check config.yaml shows the same errors without starting the bot.

docs.title: Add a recipe from chat
docs.text:
Ops add one-line reply recipes from chat, and remove any recipe:

!recipe add hug {nick} hugs {arg|default:everyone}
!recipe del hug

!recipe add checks the template, then saves it as recipes/hug.yaml.

docs.title: Set who runs it
docs.text: access: restricted or access: ops in the file sets the recipe's level. Access levels covers grants, and access.recipes in the config.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
A run takes at most 100 steps, loops included. A recipe that calls itself, directly or through another recipe, stops with the chain it took:

gamenight stopped: it calls itself: gamenight -> pick -> gamenight

docs.title: Your first bot
docs.text: This page makes a bot, gives it a dice command, tests the command and runs the bot on IRC.

docs.title: Create the bot
docs.text:
pinhook new bot gamebot

This makes the folder gamebot/:

gamebot/
├── config.yaml         the bot's settings
├── plugins/
│   └── hello.py        an example plugin
├── tests/
│   └── test_hello.py   its test
├── recipes/            commands written as YAML
├── data/               what plugins save
└── logs/

docs.title: Configure it
docs.text:
Edit gamebot/config.yaml:

nickname: 'gamebot'
server: 'irc.libera.chat'
port: 6697
ssl_required: true
channels:
  - '#gamebot-test'
ops:
  - '$a:youraccount'
bot_dir: '.'

$a:youraccount makes your services account an op, so nobody gets op powers by taking your nick. Quote channel names: YAML reads an unquoted # as the start of a comment. Configuration covers the file.

docs.title: Write a plugin
docs.text:
Save this as gamebot/plugins/dice.py:

import random

from pinhook import command


@command('roll', help='roll dice, like roll 2 20')
async def roll(ctx, count: int = 1, sides: int = 6):
    rolls = [random.randint(1, sides) for _ in range(count)]
    await ctx.reply(f'{ctx.nick} rolled {sum(rolls)} {rolls}')

Arguments come from the message, converted to their annotated types. !roll 2 20 runs roll with count=2 and sides=20. !roll two gets the usage line back:

usage: roll [count=1] [sides=6] (count must be a whole number)

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
Save this as gamebot/tests/test_dice.py:

from pinhook.testing import TestBot


def test_roll():
    bot = TestBot(plugin_dir='plugins')
    assert bot.say('!roll 3 1', nick='ana') == ['ana rolled 3 [1, 1, 1]']

Run the tests from the bot folder:

cd gamebot
pytest

TestBot runs the real bot on a fake network, with no server. TestBot covers it.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
pinhook check config.yaml
pinhook run config.yaml

check loads the config, plugins and recipes without connecting, and lists anything wrong. run connects and joins #gamebot-test. Say !roll 2 20 there.

docs.title: Change it while it runs
docs.text:
Edit plugins/dice.py, then say !reload as an op. The bot loads the new code without disconnecting. Class plugins & reload covers keeping state across a reload.
